scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Rejecting balletic fairy tales, Pina Bausch transformed choreography by asking not how people move, but what moves them.
This is Tanztheater. 20th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (43L754iMmkI)
Title card: Tanztheater · Germany · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tanztheater originated within Central European expressionist dance (Ausdruckstanz) during the 1910s and 1920s, shaped by the pedagogical ideas of François Delsarte and the cultural ferment of the Weimar Republic.
The term appeared around 1927, tied to pioneers such as Rudolf von Laban, Kurt Jooss, and Mary Wigman, who rejected the stylized conventions and fairy-tale themes of 19th-century classical ballet.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Conceived as an art of social engagement, Tanztheater rejects mere entertainment and technical showing-off in favor of humanism, politics, and emotional inquiry.
The form tackles themes drawn from philosophy, psychoanalysis, and religion.
As Pina Bausch famously articulated, the core concern of the medium is not how people move, but what moves them from within.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Tanztheater is not danced as an onstage improvisation; instead, choreographies are developed through the performers' emotional movement improvisations during rehearsals.
The dancer acts as both actor and dancer, devoid of a singular codified kinetic style.
The form relies heavily on scenic repetition, dramatic situations, gesture, and the expressive handling of time, silence, and musical phrasing.
Watch for Emotional improvisation (Bewegungen), Scenic repetition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music in Tanztheater functions through the linear management of time and silence, which together create an audible or visible musicality.
Pieces range across varied musical accompaniments, from theatrical silence to classical scores, without adhering to a single specific rhythmic framework.

Soundscapes in Tanztheater balance audible accompaniment with deliberate silence. The auditory pacing is dictated by the dramatic tension on the theatrical stage rather than strict musical dance meters.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Tanztheater stages distance themselves from classical ballet sets and tutus, placing dancers in contemporary, dramatic, or everyday environments.
Sets often incorporate specific, physically demanding environments that reflect internal human obsessions, philosophical dilemmas, and psychoanalytic states.
Performers frequently appear in ordinary dress or dramatic character attire suitable for their dual identity as dancers and actors.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include Rudolf von Laban, Kurt Jooss, and Mary Wigman, alongside Jean Weidt and Gret Palucca.
Pina Bausch served as the principal architect of its modern maturation through Tanztheater Wuppertal, aided by dramaturge Raimund Hoghe.
In West Germany, Tanztheater evolved through centers such as Wuppertal, the Bremer Theater, Schauspielhaus Bochum, and the Folkwang-Tanzstudio in Essen.
Tanztheater stems directly from German Ausdruckstanz and Central European modern dance, shaped by early modern pioneers like François Delsarte and Isadora Duncan.
